questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient admitted with STEMI, now status-post CABG, and with a complicated hospital course thereafter, including prolonged respiratory failure requiring tracheostomy and gastrostomy tube placements, who also received several days of broad-spectrum antibiotics postoperatively because of shock, and concern for possible sepsis, is now having increasing supplemental oxygen requirement and fever. His chest radiograph shows diffuse pulmonary opacities, worst in the right-lower lobe. His nurse also has noted increasingly profuse and purulent tracheal secretions. He was started on linezolid and meropenem, but after 2 days he was still having fevers, and his respiratory status continued to worsen. Tracheal aspirate culture is now growing an organism that was identified as an oxidase-positive, nonfermenting gram-negative bacillus.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia This patient has hospital-acquired pneumonia and did not demonstrate clinical improvement on broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. He has multiple risk factors for development of drug-resistant pathogens, including his prolonged ICU stay and antecedent antibiotic therapy. Linezolid and meropenem would provide more than adequate activity against most gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens, including those that would produce extended-spectrum β-lactamases. Stenotrophomonas can be a cause of HAP , is intrinsically resistant to the antibiotic agents that he has been receiving, and is a nonfermenting gram-negative bacillus that is oxidase-positive. Other nonfermenting, oxidase-positive gram-negative bacilli include Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Achromobacter, and Burkholderia, among others.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q31

questions.question: Shortest duration for
questions.model_answer: Shortest recommended durations: Cellulitis - 5 days; Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis - 5-7 days (e.g., with a fluoroquinolone); Peritonsillar abscess (comparable to adult CAP context) - 5-7 days after drainage; Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) - 7 days; Frontal (bacterial) brain abscess - typically 4-6 weeks of IV therapy (shortest end of the accepted range), longer than the other listed infections given the difficulty of source control and CNS penetration requirements.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA duration-of-therapy guidance for cellulitis, pyelonephritis, and VAP is not covered in this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: For the following conditions, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics: Retropharyngeal abscess on Peds exam, VAP on adult exam, CAP, Cellulitis, Uncomplicated pyelonephritis.

parts.text: For each condition, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics.

cohort_answer.text: Retropharyngeal abscess 14 days (UTD, Redbook); VAP 7 days; CAP 5 days; Cellulitis 5 days; Uncomplicated pyelo 7 days. Resource: AMMI Duration Paper https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9615468/

questions.question: A patient in the ICU develops a ventilator-associated pneumonia. BAL sample grows Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

parts.text: Name FOUR treatments (each from different antimicrobial classes) that can be used for this infection? – (2016; 2019)

questions.question: Write the shortest duration of therapy for VAP, CAP, Cellulitis, Uncomplicated Pyelo

cohort_answer.text: VAP: 3 days (IDSA 2016). CAP: 3 days (IDSA 2019). Cellulitis: 5 days (IDSA 2014). Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 5 days (IDSA 2010; fluoroquinolones only for 5d if local resistance <10%).

questions.question: There is a patient who is intubated and develops VAP due to Stenotrophomonas (severity not specified). He is on Meropenem.

parts.text: What is the best empiric therapy for this infection?
He is unable to tolerate that drug. Name two non-beta lactam antibiotic alternatives you can use that have relatively little toxicity

cohort_answer.text: Meropenem inappropriate: Intrinsic resistance (L1 metallo beta-lactamase); S. maltophilia carries numerous resistance genes/mutations - L1 hydrolyzes penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems (not aztreonam), L2 has extended cephalosporin activity and hydrolyzes aztreonam; intrinsic aminoglycoside resistance via chromosomal acetyl transferase enzymes; multidrug efflux pumps reduce TMP-SMX, tetracycline, fluoroquinolone activity, chromosomal Smqnr genes further reduce fluoroquinolone effectiveness. Best empiric therapy (IDSA 2023 Guidance): 1) Use of 2 agents: TMP-SMX, minocycline/tigecycline, cefiderocol or levofloxacin; 2) Combination of ceftazidime-avibactam and aztreonam when significant instability or intolerance/inactivity of other agents identified. Alternatives if intolerant: Levofloxacin; Minocycline > Tigecycline
